name: Newcastle, NSW
title: Newcastle, NSW Bulk Carrier Gauging | Hold & Hopper UTM
description: Bulk carrier thickness gauging at Newcastle, NSW: holds, hopper and topside tanks, hatch covers and ballast tanks on coal ships at anchor or at the berth.
h1: Hold and Tank Thickness Gauging for Bulk Carriers at Newcastle, NSW
intro: Newcastle, at the mouth of the Hunter River, is the world's largest coal export port, and its traffic is overwhelmingly Capesize, Panamax and smaller bulk carriers, with grain, alumina, fertiliser and fuel ships alongside. Ships commonly wait at the offshore anchorage for a loading slot, and both the wait and the loading stay can be used to gauge holds, hopper plating and ballast tanks. The team is sent from India to the ship for each job, as Atlantis has no base anywhere in New South Wales.

highlights.h: Hold and hopper wastage from coal
highlights.p: Coal cargoes are often moist and can be acidic, and years of loading leave hold frames, lower brackets, hopper plating and tank tops wasted and pitted. Newcastle is where many of the ships that carry it can be held still long enough to measure that wastage before a survey, a charter or a sale.

When the coal chain is busy, bulk carriers wait at the fair-weather anchorage off the port for their loading slot. In settled conditions that wait can be used for ballast tank and empty-hold gauging, provided the agent can arrange the boat transfer and the ship is not called in to berth.

Holds arrive clean and empty for loading, which is the best moment to measure frames, brackets and shell plating. Gauging can be sequenced with the hold cleanliness inspection, so readings in each hold are taken before the shiploader reaches it.

port.h: Hunter River entrance, the coal terminals and the fair-weather anchorage
p: Newcastle Harbour is formed by the lower Hunter River, entered between breakwaters beside Nobbys Head, with the city on the southern shore and the coal terminals at Carrington and on Kooragang Island across the harbour channels. The entrance is narrow and exposed to the Tasman Sea, and ships move in and out under compulsory pilotage provided by the Port Authority of New South Wales, which also runs Newcastle VTS; pilots board by boat or by helicopter. The Port of Newcastle company manages the port's land and berths under a long-term lease, and every large bulk carrier needs tugs to turn and berth in the harbour's tight channels. Ships arriving for coal usually wait at the fair-weather anchorage offshore until a berth and their cargo are ready.

Coal is the port's purpose. Three loading terminals, two run by Port Waratah Coal Services at Carrington and Kooragang and one by Newcastle Coal Infrastructure Group on Kooragang Island, ship thermal and metallurgical coal from the Hunter Valley and Gunnedah basin mines to Japan, Korea, Taiwan, China, India and South-East Asia. Capesize and Panamax bulk carriers make up most of those calls, with Supramax and smaller ships for part cargoes. Other berths, including those at Mayfield and Dyke Point, handle grain, alumina, fertiliser, ore concentrates and general cargo, and chemical and product tankers bring fuel into the region. Cruise ships call during the summer season, and the harbour is home to the tugs and pilot vessels that serve all of this traffic.

The anchorage lies in open water south of the port entrance, at least three nautical miles off the coast, with no allocated berths and a seabed where holding has to be checked. Main engines must stay ready while a ship is anchored, and when a severe weather warning is issued or the swell builds, the harbour master's directions require ships to weigh anchor and put to sea. East Coast Lows, most frequent from late autumn into winter, are the usual cause; the grounding of a waiting bulk carrier on Nobbys Beach in June 2007 is the event every master here knows. In fine weather a ship may lie at anchor for days. Loading time alongside depends on the parcel size and the terminal's stockpile sequence, and heavy rain in the Hunter catchment can bring strong outflow in the river.

facilities.h: Where bulk carriers at Newcastle can be gauged
p: Most Newcastle gauging happens alongside or at anchor. At a coal berth the holds are loaded in sequence, so hold work has to be done in the hours after arrival, once the holds have been passed clean and before the shiploader reaches them; ballast, topside and hopper tanks remain accessible as deballasting allows. At anchor, a boat arranged by the agent can take the team out in settled weather, and empty holds and ballast tanks can be measured without the pressure of loading, though the call to berth or an order to sea can come at short notice. Coal dust and the terminals' safety rules govern deck work, and anyone without a Maritime Security Identification Card is escorted inside security zones.

Newcastle has no drydock for ships of the size it loads. A Capesize or Panamax bulk carrier in the coal trade docks in Asia, which makes Newcastle a natural place to take readings for a pre-docking steel estimate on a ship about to head back north. Tugs, pilot boats, dredgers and workboats based in the harbour are maintained on local slipways and by ship repairers working in the port, and those smaller craft can be gauged when they are out of the water.
list: Port Waratah coal terminals at Carrington and Kooragang — holds, hopper and topside tanks on Capesize and Panamax bulk carriers, timed to the loading sequence.
Newcastle Coal Infrastructure Group terminal, Kooragang Island — the same bulk carrier work, coordinated with the terminal's berth schedule.
Mayfield and Dyke berths — grain, alumina, fertiliser and general cargo ships; hold and tank gauging during loading or discharge.
Fuel and chemical tanker berths — ballast tanks, deck structure and piping measured under the terminal's rules.
Fair-weather anchorage offshore — empty-hold and ballast tank gauging on ships waiting for a berth, in settled conditions.
Harbour slipways — tugs, pilot boats and workboats out of the water.

context.h: AMSA, charterers' vetting and the coal trade
p: AMSA carries out port state control at Newcastle under Australia's membership of the Tokyo MoU and the Indian Ocean MoU, and bulk carriers are the ships its surveyors see most often here. Structural defects in holds, hatch covers and ballast tanks can lead to detention, so a ship whose last renewal survey left wastage close to the allowable limits arrives better prepared with recent readings and repair records on board. The close-up survey and thickness measurement regime for bulk carriers was itself a response to the bulk carrier losses of the 1990s, many of them ships in heavy, dense cargo trades of the kind Australia's export ports serve.

Commercial vetting matters as much as port state control. Miners, traders and charterers in the Australian dry bulk trades screen ships before fixing them, and RightShip ratings and inspections are widely used for that purpose; evidence of structural condition, including recent thickness readings and steel renewal records, supports an older ship's acceptability. International arrivals must also report their biofouling management to the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry before entering Australian waters, and long waits at anchor in warm water encourage hull fouling, which matters both for that reporting and for the ship's fuel consumption on the return voyage.

jobs.h: Gauging jobs we see on bulk carriers at Newcastle
jobs.p: Almost every Newcastle job is a bulk carrier job. Owners ask for hold frame, bracket and hopper plating readings ahead of an intermediate or renewal survey, so steel renewal can be quantified before the ship reaches a yard; buyers ask for a pre-purchase inspection of holds, ballast tanks and hatch covers while the seller's ship waits to load; charterers and managers ask for condition gauging to support a vetting inspection or a CAP rating on an older ship. The scope is planned around the loading slot, which can move, so we agree with the superintendent which spaces come first and which can wait for time at anchor. The team mobilises from India once the visa and the ship's arrival window are confirmed, and the report follows the class formats.
list: Hold frame and lower bracket gauging on a Capesize at anchor off Newcastle, ahead of its third renewal survey in Asia.
Pre-purchase inspection of a Panamax's holds, hatch covers and ballast tanks while it waits for a coal berth.
CAP gauging on an ageing Supramax for a charterer's vetting requirement, split between anchorage and berth time.
Topside and hopper tank gauging during deballasting at a Kooragang coal berth.
Hatch coaming and cover plating gauging, with magnetic particle checks at the coaming brackets, on a grain carrier at Mayfield.

logistics: The nearest airport is Newcastle Airport at Williamtown, north of the city, which mainly has domestic flights; international arrivals usually come through Sydney and continue by domestic flight or by road up the coast. Indian nationals need an Australian visa that covers short-term specialist work, applied for as soon as the ship's arrival window is known because processing times vary. The ship's agent arranges terminal access, escorts within security zones, biosecurity clearance checks and any boat to the anchorage.

faqs.q: Can a bulk carrier be gauged at the Newcastle anchorage?
faqs.a: In settled weather, yes. The agent arranges a boat, and with holds empty and ballast tanks accessible a waiting ship offers good working conditions, often better than at the berth. The risks are the open-sea transfer, a call to berth, or a harbour master's order to put to sea when the weather turns, so we plan the scope in priority order and finish anything outstanding alongside.

faqs.q: How much hold gauging is possible once loading starts?
faqs.a: Not much in the holds being loaded. Hold work is best done between arrival and the start of loading, or at anchor beforehand, once the holds have been passed for cleanliness. When the shiploader is working, the team concentrates on ballast, topside and hopper tanks, deck plating and hatch coamings, coordinated with the chief officer's loading and deballasting plan.

faqs.q: Can a ship dock for steel renewal in Newcastle?
faqs.a: Not a ship of the size that loads coal here. Bulk carriers in this trade dock in Asian yards, and the usual approach is to gauge in Newcastle, at anchor or alongside, and send the yard a measured steel estimate with the specification. Harbour craft are the exception: tugs, pilot boats and workboats are maintained locally and can be gauged on the slip.

faqs.q: What happens to a gauging plan when an East Coast Low arrives?
faqs.a: Work at anchor stops, and ships are directed to sea until the weather passes, which can shift the whole call by days. Once a ship is inside the harbour, tank work carries on in bad weather. We keep travel arrangements flexible during the late autumn and winter months and agree with the superintendent in advance how a delayed berthing will be handled.
